scope: spec check: the diagnostic codes, their severities, the --ci cold-rebuild gate, which severity exits 1, and the spec glossary round-trip that GLOSSARY_DRIFT enforces. Belongs here: diagnostic codes and severities; the --ci gate; the exit-1 contract. Does not belong here: member discovery (INIT). Boundary case: NO_SPEC_CONFIG is emitted by discovery, but its severity is CHCK's.

requirements.statement: spec check reports cross-repo integrity diagnostics (dangling, superseded-referenced, orphan, unverified, drift) and exits non-zero on error-severity rows under --ci.
requirements.why: The gate; it catches all the planted mess.

requirements.statement: spec check --ci builds fresh and is correct without trusting any cached or warm index.
requirements.why: Speed optimizations must never make correctness depend on a stale index.

requirements.statement: NO_SPEC_CONFIG is warning severity: spec check --ci does not fail on it.
requirements.why: A user may legitimately keep unrelated sibling repos in the same parent directory.

requirements.statement: spec check reports UNDEFINED_TERM (error) when a requirement's cites entry resolves to no term and ORPHAN_TERM (warning) for an Active term that no requirement cites
requirements.why: the only-allowed-jargon rule becomes mechanically checkable and glossary rot is surfaced, without a freshly-migrated uncited term redding the gate (ORPHAN_TERM is warning-only)

requirements.statement: spec check reports TERM_DRIFT (warning) when a requirement's cites pin lags the cited term's current version after an in-place spec term revise, and SUPERSEDED_TERM_REFERENCED (error) when a citation references a superseded term id, until re-confirmed via spec term confirm (which re-pins, and re-points to the successor on supersession).
requirements.why: term drift is the member-pin drift model replayed one level up (req to term): a citation implicitly pins the term version it was confirmed against; re-confirmation is explicit via spec term confirm, and the term_drift VIEW clones the drift VIEW predicate so there is one predicate in one place.

requirements.statement: GLOSSARY.md is migrated into TERM-001..N and then generated from the term store byte-stably, and a CI fence fails if the committed GLOSSARY.md diverges from the generated output.
requirements.why: The human view of the glossary must not drift from the canonical terms — generation is a deterministic projection of the store, fenced in CI.

requirements.statement: If a code tag references a deprecated requirement, then spec check shall report DEPRECATED_REFERENCED as an error.
requirements.why: Code claiming to implement an end-of-life promise is a disagreement between spec and code that otherwise stays invisible — the SUPERSEDED_REFERENCED analogue for the other terminal status.

requirements.statement: If a domain declares the ears grammar and an Active or Draft statement does not match one of the five EARS shapes, then spec check shall report STATEMENT_GRAMMAR at the domain's declared severity, defaulting to warning.
requirements.why: Vague statements read as fine and fail as requirements — without a mechanical check the burn-down list is invisible and new word salad enters unnoticed.

requirements.statement: If a code tag references a Draft requirement, then spec check shall report DRAFT_REFERENCED as a warning.
requirements.why: Code shipped against a promise nobody approved yet is invisible otherwise — the draft quietly becomes de-facto truth without ever being accepted.

requirements.statement: If the committed GLOSSARY.md does not byte-match the glossary generated from the TERM store, then spec check shall report GLOSSARY_DRIFT as a warning.
requirements.why: Only this repo's own CI fence caught glossary drift before; an adopter's human view of the terms could lie forever under a green gate.

requirements.statement: While the platform is a git repository with a resolvable HEAD, spec check shall report REQUIREMENT_REMOVED for any requirement present at HEAD that is absent from the working tree without a supersession in the same change, with no flag required.
requirements.why: A deleted requirement was invisible to a plain spec check unless the opt-in --base flag was wired in CI — the biggest disagreement the tool exists to catch defaulted to off.

requirements.statement: The spec check command shall report integrity diagnostics across every member repo, each row carrying a code, a severity, and the offending location.
requirements.why: Spec-code disagreements — dangling tags, superseded references, orphan and unverified requirements — stay invisible without one command that surfaces them all.

requirements.statement: When spec check finds at least one error-severity diagnostic, the command shall exit 1; warnings alone leave the exit at 0.
requirements.why: CI branches on the exit code, not the output text; without this contract a red finding sails through the gate unnoticed.

requirements.statement: When spec check runs with --ci, the command shall delete the existing index and rebuild it cold before evaluating diagnostics.
requirements.why: A warm index can predate the latest spec and tag edits, so the gate would pass or fail against stale truth.

requirements.statement: When spec check finds a sibling directory without a spec-engine.member.json, the command shall report NO_SPEC_CONFIG at warning severity, so the finding alone never fails the --ci gate.
requirements.why: Unrelated sibling repos in the same parent directory are legitimate; failing the gate on them would force every neighbor to join the platform.

requirements.statement: If a requirement's cites entry resolves to no term, then spec check shall report UNDEFINED_TERM as an error.
requirements.why: A requirement leaning on jargon no reader can look up is unreviewable; as a warning the broken citation would ship under a green gate.

requirements.statement: If an Active term is cited by no requirement, then spec check shall report ORPHAN_TERM as a warning.
requirements.why: Uncited terms accumulate as glossary rot nobody sees; at error severity a freshly-migrated glossary would red the gate before any citation could exist.

requirements.statement: If a requirement's citation pins an older version than the cited term's current version, then spec check shall report TERM_DRIFT as a warning until spec term confirm re-pins it.
requirements.why: An in-place definition revision can change the meaning of every citing requirement; without a signal nobody re-reads them, while an error would block builds on a wording tweak.

requirements.statement: If a requirement cites a superseded term id, then spec check shall report SUPERSEDED_TERM_REFERENCED as an error until spec term confirm re-points the citation to the successor.
requirements.why: A requirement defined by a dead term no longer means what it appears to mean; as a warning it would ship anyway.

requirements.statement: When spec glossary runs, the command shall regenerate GLOSSARY.md from the term store deterministically, byte-identical across runs over the same store.
requirements.why: A generator with nondeterministic output makes drift detection impossible — every regeneration would itself look like drift.

requirements.statement: When spec glossary --migrate runs, the command shall parse each committed GLOSSARY.md bullet into a term entry in document order, skipping when the term store already holds entries.
requirements.why: Re-running a migration that re-mints ids would duplicate every term; without the parser the glossary's terms never become canonical data at all.

requirements.statement: When spec glossary --check runs and the committed GLOSSARY.md differs byte-for-byte from the generated output, the command shall exit 1.
requirements.why: The human view of the terms can silently diverge from the canonical store; only a failing exit code makes that drift block a merge.

requirements.statement: While the platform is a git repository with a resolvable HEAD, spec check shall report REQUIREMENT_REMOVED for any requirement present at HEAD that is absent from the working tree without a supersession in the same change, with no flag required.
requirements.why: Without default-on detection, a deleted requirement is invisible to a plain spec check — the biggest disagreement the tool exists to catch goes unreported.

requirements.statement: If the committed GLOSSARY.md does not byte-match the glossary generated from the TERM store, then spec check shall report GLOSSARY_DRIFT as a warning.
requirements.why: Without the diagnostic, an adopter's committed glossary can misstate the canonical terms indefinitely under a green gate.

requirements.statement: When spec check finds a sibling directory without a spec-engine.member.json, the command shall report NO_SPEC_CONFIG at warning severity.
requirements.why: Unrelated sibling repos in the same parent directory are legitimate; failing the gate on them would force every neighbor to join the platform.

requirements.statement: If an Active or Draft requirement's livesIn entry does not resolve to a file under the platform root, then spec check shall report BROKEN_FILE_REF at error severity.
requirements.why: A requirement that points at a file which is not there is a broken link nobody can see; without the check, livesIn is write-only text that CI can never verify.

requirements.statement: Where a requirement is superseded or deprecated, spec check shall not report BROKEN_FILE_REF for its livesIn entries.
requirements.why: The file a retired requirement used to live in is expected to be gone, so judging history would make every cleanup red the gate.

requirements.statement: The system shall derive BROKEN_FILE_REF from livesIn entries only and never from @-refs appearing in statement or why text.
requirements.why: The @-ref grammar's only path test is that the token contains a slash, which a scoped npm package name also passes, so a text-wide check reports @spec-engine/spec-engine as a missing file.

requirements.statement: If a requirement's supersedes pointer names an id that does not exist or names the requirement itself, then spec check shall report BROKEN_SUPERSEDE at error severity.
requirements.why: The loss gates honor supersedes as a removal exemption, so an unchecked forward pointer is the one field a hand-edit can use to excuse deleting a requirement.

requirements.statement: The AGENTS.md spec check reference shall list every diagnostic code the engine can emit and no other, so an agent reading the reference sees the same code set the command produces.
requirements.why: An agent branching on a code missing from the reference, or on one that no longer exists, misreads the gate.

requirements.statement: When platform-map reports a diagnostic for the platform that is an error or a warning, or an info that means a repository's tags go unscanned, spec check shall surface it as a diagnostic row with the platform-map code, so a broken platform declaration fails the same gate a broken requirement does.
requirements.why: A platform whose declaration is broken silently scans the wrong set of repositories, and a separate tool's check that CI never runs is no gate.

requirements.statement: The spec engine shall raise ORPHAN_REQ and UNVERIFIED_REQ only for Active requirements, and shall count only Active requirements in the coverage report.
requirements.why: A draft is a promise not yet agreed; reporting it as an orphan or counting it as uncovered would read an unreviewed candidate as a broken commitment.

requirements.statement: If a verifying @spec tag references a Draft requirement, then spec check shall report DRAFT_REFERENCED at error severity.
requirements.why: A test that claims an unaccepted promise asserts behaviour nobody agreed to.

requirements.statement: If an implementing or documenting @spec tag references a Draft requirement, then spec check shall report DRAFT_REFERENCED at warning severity.
requirements.why: Specifying behaviour that already ships is the ordinary retro-specification state; failing on it blocks every adopter doing it.

requirements.statement: The spec check command shall report UNVERIFIED_REQ at warning severity by default.
requirements.why: An implemented requirement with no test is incomplete, not broken; failing the gate on it makes adopters wrap check in a severity filter or stop running it.

requirements.statement: When spec-engine/check.json declares a severity rule for a diagnostic code, spec check shall grade every row of that code to the rule's severity of error, warning, or off.
requirements.why: Which diagnostic blocks a merge is adopter policy; a wrapper that re-grades check --json drifts from the engine.

requirements.statement: When a severity rule carries a match list of domain keys or requirement ids, spec check shall apply it only to rows whose requirement is listed or carries a listed key, the most specific rule winning.
requirements.why: A tests-required ledger is a set of ids and domains that a code-wide rule cannot express.

requirements.statement: When a diagnostic row is graded off, spec check shall omit it from every output.
requirements.why: A row the adopter declared irrelevant trains readers to ignore the report.

requirements.statement: If spec-engine/check.json fails its schema, then spec check shall exit 2 naming the file and the failing path.
requirements.why: A misspelled rule that is silently ignored looks like a rule in force.

requirements.statement: If a domain declares the ears grammar and the text after the first shall in an Active or Draft statement contains a semicolon followed by whitespace, then spec check shall report STATEMENT_GRAMMAR at the domain's declared severity.
requirements.why: A semicolon after the result usually chains a second behavior, which no single test proves, so a requirement passes review while half of it goes untested.

requirements.statement: If a domain declares the ears grammar and an Active or Draft statement's result continues with a comma-and clause that names its own subject before another shall, then spec check shall report STATEMENT_GRAMMAR at the domain's declared severity.
requirements.why: A second subject with its own shall is a second promise hiding in one id, so supersession and coverage track two behaviors as one.

requirements.statement: If a domain declares the ears grammar and an Active or Draft statement carries a rationale connective, then spec check shall report STATEMENT_GRAMMAR at the domain's declared severity.
requirements.why: Rationale in the statement duplicates the why field and drifts from it, so a reader gets two reasons and the statement stops being a testable promise.

requirements.statement: When spec check finds at least one error-severity diagnostic, the command shall exit 1.
requirements.why: CI branches on the exit code, not the output text; without this contract a red finding sails through the gate unnoticed.

requirements.statement: When spec check finds only warning-severity diagnostics, the command shall exit 0.
requirements.why: A warning is advisory; failing the exit on warnings alone turns every advisory into a CI failure and teaches teams to silence the check.

requirements.statement: If an Active or Draft requirement's livesIn or verifiedIn entry does not resolve to a file under the platform root, then spec check shall report BROKEN_FILE_REF at error severity.
requirements.why: A requirement that points at a file which is not there is a broken link nobody can see; without the check, livesIn is write-only text that CI can never verify.

requirements.statement: When an Active requirement's livesIn entry resolves to a file the scanner reads and that file holds no implementing or documenting tag for the requirement, spec check shall report UNIMPLEMENTED_IN_FILE at warning severity by default, or at the severity check.json configures for the code.
requirements.why: A location claim that silently stops carrying its tag keeps the gate green while the claim is false; one in four of this platform's own entries had drifted that way unreported.

requirements.statement: When an Active requirement's verifiedIn entry resolves to a file the scanner reads and that file holds no verifying tag for the requirement, spec check shall report UNVERIFIED_IN_FILE at warning severity by default, or at the severity check.json configures for the code.
requirements.why: A named test file that does not claim the requirement is a proof nobody runs; without the check an adopter keeps a per-file ledger outside the CLI to enforce it.

requirements.statement: When check.json configures statement rules, every surface shall honor its maximum length, jargon list, exempt names, and per-rule severity, with off turning a rule off everywhere.
requirements.why: A rule tuned in one place and not another lets the write path and the check disagree on the same statement.

requirements.statement: When an Active statement breaks a rule, spec check shall report STATEMENT_RULES at warning severity by default, one row per rule per statement.
requirements.why: Statements written before the rules existed would otherwise sit in the book unreported until someone happens to edit them.

requirements.statement: spec lint shall print every finding for the platform, one domain, or one requirement, and exit 1 when there is any.
requirements.why: Without an on-demand report scoped to the work at hand, a sweep has no way to see what is left or prove it is finished.

requirements.statement: spec lint shall check Active requirements by default and Draft requirements too under --all.
requirements.why: A draft that breaks a rule is refused only at accept, so an author reviewing drafts early needs a way to see those findings first.

requirements.statement: Where --json, spec lint shall print the findings as a sorted array.
requirements.why: An agent sweeping the book parses the findings, and unsorted output makes every run look like a change.
